items.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012
items.q: Cootie Williams plays the five-one, and the first thing you hear against this tonic note is G flat 7 [plays piano].

ctx.x: Yeah. So there’s a great example. So the thing that I found with Clare and Duke is that a lot of times when I would find I’d hear this voice and go oh, what is that? Sometimes it would be something that I wouldn’t think of playing, and sometimes I’d realize oh it’s just the same voicing but the notes are rearranged so it gets a different color. We were talking about improvising and using a major seventh on a dominant chord, it’s the same thing with writing. Like at the end of “Concerto for Cootie,” after you hear…

he’s on the flat sixth [plays piano]. And the clarinet’s up here but with the alto. Cootie Williams plays the five-one, and the first thing you hear against this tonic note is G flat 7 [plays piano]. So that’s not only a way of making a major seventh on a dominant seventh sound great, but it makes that F 6 chord that comes afterwards sound great too. Because it’s not the chords that you use, it’s how you get there and where you go from there. So one of the things I also try to impart to the students as much as…
You made me think of a question I was going to ask about being self-indulgent when you improvise.
